Cybersecurity company Jamf has discovered that a fake Mac installer disguised as the Zoom video conferencing software uses a clever method to bypass Gatekeeper, circumventing Apple's defence mechanism against malware.

The malware does indeed install Zoom, but at the same time it plants a data-stealing program that collects user information and transmits it to the attacker's servers...

Normally, when you attempt to install a Mac application that has not been notarised by Apple, macOS will refuse to open it. Although there are ways around this restriction, the steps involved are rather cumbersome, so attackers must find a way to persuade users to carry out those steps themselves.

Jamf has named this malware CloudSyncD. The criminals behind it have found a clever method that makes the whole process appear more legitimate to users. The application's installer loader contains a background image with instructions, as shown in the image above.

You have to admire their creativity.

Once the malware is successfully installed, it can record the user's keystrokes and transmit the data to the attacker every few seconds.

As always, you should only install Mac applications from the official Mac App Store or from the websites of developers you trust.
